chapters.title: Galatians 1 — No other gospel and Paul's calling
chapters.historicalContext: Galatia's churches faced teachers who urged Gentile believers to adopt circumcision and other boundary markers. Paul writes with urgency because the gospel of grace and the unity of the churches are at stake.
chapters.overview: Paul defends the divine source of his apostleship and insists that the message he proclaimed was not received from human authority. He recounts his former life, his encounter with Christ, and his early ministry.
chapters.studyObservation: The opening rebuke is unusually direct because the issue is not a minor disagreement but a distortion of the gospel. Paul's story serves the argument that the message rests on God's revelation in Christ.
chapters.connectionNotes: Read with chapters 2–3, where Paul explains the Jerusalem meeting, justification, and Abraham's promise. Compare Paul's account with Acts 9 and 15 while noting each author's purpose.
chapters.lifeApplication: Hold firmly to the good news of Christ and examine teachings that add human achievements as conditions for acceptance by God. Let a changed life testify to grace.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Paul's defence of his calling is not a licence for leaders to reject accountability. His message is tested in relationship with other apostles and by its faithfulness to Christ.
chapters.readingNote: Notice how quickly Paul moves from greeting to warning, then follow how his personal history supports the central gospel claim.
studyQuestions: Why is Paul alarmed by the message spreading in Galatia?
How does Paul's story support his claim about the gospel?
How can believers test teaching without making a leader unquestionable?

chapters.title: Galatians 2 — The gospel confirmed and justification by faith
chapters.historicalContext: Paul describes a later visit to Jerusalem, where the gospel to the Gentiles was recognised. He also recounts confronting Peter at Antioch when Peter withdrew from table fellowship with Gentile believers.
chapters.overview: The chapter emphasises that people are justified through faith in Jesus Christ, not by works of the law. Paul's confrontation with Peter shows that conduct must agree with the truth of the gospel.
chapters.studyObservation: The dispute at Antioch was not merely about food customs; withdrawal threatened the equal standing and fellowship of Gentile believers. Gospel truth has visible communal consequences.
chapters.connectionNotes: Connect this chapter with Acts 15 and Romans 3–4. Read the statement about Christ living in Paul with the fruit-of-the-Spirit teaching in chapter 5.
chapters.lifeApplication: Let the gospel shape how you welcome and treat others. Refuse practices that make ethnicity, status, or religious performance a basis for superiority in Christ's community.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Paul's account should not be flattened into a claim that every disagreement must be handled publicly. The specific issue involved public conduct that contradicted the gospel and harmed shared fellowship.
chapters.readingNote: Trace the movement from Jerusalem's recognition of Paul's mission to the Antioch incident, then observe how the theological explanation answers the practical conflict.
studyQuestions: What did the Jerusalem leaders recognise about Paul's mission?
Why did Peter's withdrawal at Antioch matter for the gospel?
How does faith in Christ reshape belonging and shared fellowship?

chapters.title: Galatians 3 — Faith, the Spirit, Abraham, and the promise
chapters.historicalContext: Paul appeals to the Galatians' experience of receiving the Spirit and to Scripture's account of Abraham. He addresses whether Gentile believers must come under the law to share in God's promise.
chapters.overview: The Spirit is received through hearing with faith. Abraham's blessing reaches the nations through Christ, and the law has a distinct role in the story leading to the promised offspring.
chapters.studyObservation: Paul's argument honours the law's place in salvation history while denying that it can replace the promise or become the basis of justification. The promise precedes the law.
chapters.connectionNotes: Read Genesis 12, 15, and 17 alongside this chapter, then continue into chapter 4 where Paul develops the language of adoption and inheritance.
chapters.lifeApplication: Trust God's promise rather than trying to earn acceptance through performance. Welcome fellow believers as heirs of the promise and live from the Spirit's work.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: The chapter's contrast does not mean God's law is evil or that the Old Testament should be discarded. Paul argues about the law's role in relation to the promise fulfilled in Christ.
chapters.readingNote: Follow Paul's questions about the Spirit and Abraham, and note the distinction between receiving a promise and trying to secure it through human achievement.
studyQuestions: How does Abraham's faith support Paul's argument?
What role does Paul assign to the law in the story of the promise?
What does being one in Christ mean for divisions of status and identity?

chapters.title: Galatians 4 — Adoption, freedom, and the danger of returning to bondage
chapters.historicalContext: Paul continues the inheritance theme, explaining that Christ came in the fullness of time to redeem those under the law so they might receive adoption. He expresses pastoral concern that the Galatians may return to spiritual slavery.
chapters.overview: Believers receive the Spirit of God's Son and can cry, 'Abba, Father.' Paul uses the story of Hagar and Sarah allegorically to contrast slavery and freedom, urging the church to live as children of promise.
chapters.studyObservation: The central pastoral concern is that those who have received adoption should not surrender their freedom to a system that makes status depend on law observance. Paul's allegory serves this argument.
chapters.connectionNotes: Read the promise to Abraham in Genesis 16–21 and compare the adoption language with Romans 8:14–17. Chapter 5 continues the call to stand in freedom.
chapters.lifeApplication: Live from the identity God gives rather than seeking security through religious status. Receive the Spirit's assurance and care for believers who are vulnerable or easily pressured.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Paul's allegorical use of Hagar and Sarah must not be turned into contempt toward Jewish people or used to justify hostility. The passage addresses covenant arguments within the early church.
chapters.readingNote: Notice Paul's shift from theological explanation to affectionate appeal, and ask why he is so concerned about the Galatians' return to former patterns.
studyQuestions: What does adoption through Christ mean in Paul's argument?
Why does Paul fear that the Galatians are returning to bondage?
How should freedom shape the way believers treat one another?

chapters.title: Galatians 5 — Freedom expressed through love and the fruit of the Spirit
chapters.historicalContext: Paul urges the Galatians to stand firm in the freedom Christ has given. He rejects circumcision as a requirement for justification and explains that Christian freedom is expressed through love and life in the Spirit.
chapters.overview: Faith works through love. The Spirit leads believers away from destructive works of the flesh and produces a character marked by love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control.
chapters.studyObservation: Freedom is neither legalistic self-justification nor permission for selfishness. Paul holds together freedom from the law as a basis of status and responsibility to love one's neighbour.
chapters.connectionNotes: Connect the fruit of the Spirit with Jesus' teaching about abiding in him in John 15 and with the love chapter in 1 Corinthians 13. Chapter 6 shows how spiritual life is practised in community.
chapters.lifeApplication: Use freedom to serve others in love. Invite the Spirit to shape character and relationships, and practise the fruit of the Spirit in ordinary decisions.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: The works-of-the-flesh list is not a tool for condemning people selectively. The fruit of the Spirit is a description of Spirit-formed character, not a checklist for self-righteous comparison.
chapters.readingNote: Notice the contrast between biting and devouring one another and serving one another through love; then compare the two lists of conduct.
studyQuestions: How does Christian freedom differ from self-indulgence?
What does it mean to walk by the Spirit?
Which aspects of the fruit of the Spirit need to become more visible in community life?

chapters.title: Galatians 6 — Bearing burdens, sowing to the Spirit, and the new creation
chapters.historicalContext: Paul concludes with practical instructions for restoring those caught in wrongdoing, bearing one another's burdens, and supporting teachers. He contrasts sowing to the flesh with sowing to the Spirit and returns to the cross.
chapters.overview: The law of Christ is fulfilled in mutual care. Believers are called to humility, perseverance in doing good, and boasting only in the cross, through which the old measures of status lose their power.
chapters.studyObservation: Restoration requires gentleness and self-watchfulness. The principle of sowing and reaping concerns the moral direction and fruit of life, not a mechanical guarantee of immediate outcomes.
chapters.connectionNotes: Read the burden-bearing instruction alongside Romans 15:1–2 and the new-creation theme alongside 2 Corinthians 5:17. The closing emphasis gathers the letter's argument about cross-shaped identity.
chapters.lifeApplication: Help restore others gently, carry burdens together, and continue doing good without growing weary. Let the cross—not outward religious display—define your confidence.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: The sowing-and-reaping principle should not be used to blame sufferers for every hardship or promise instant prosperity. Paul's focus is perseverance, moral formation, and the final harvest.
chapters.readingNote: Observe how Paul's final practical instructions translate freedom and the Spirit's fruit into community care, humility, and perseverance.
studyQuestions: How should a believer restore someone caught in wrongdoing?
What does it mean to sow to the Spirit?
Why does Paul conclude by boasting only in the cross and new creation?
